articles.title: A member of one body

claims.t: Everything that reasons shares one reason, as limbs share one body, citizens one city, and every lit place one sun.
claims.shared: Four pictures (body, city, sunlight, soul) with one structure: a single thing present in many, and not split by being shared.

support.quote: As several members in one body united, so are reasonable creatures in a body divided and dispersed
gives: as limbs share one body
Everything that reasons
support.follows: Reasoning beings relate to one another as the parts of one body do.

support.quote: then are we fellow-citizens. If so, then are we partners in some one commonweal. If so, then the world is as it were a city.
gives: citizens one city
support.note: The last step of a chain that starts from reason being common to all.
support.follows: We are fellow citizens, partners in one commonwealth, and the world is like a city.

support.quote: There is but one light of the sun, though it be intercepted by walls and mountains
gives: every lit place one sun
support.follows: The light of the sun is one, even where walls and mountains block it.

support.quote: So is there but one common intellectual soul, though it seem to be divided.
gives: shares one reason
support.follows: There is one common reasoning soul, even though it seems to be divided.

support.quote: of all that are reasonable, but one reasonable soul, divided betwixt them all
gives: shares one reason
Everything that reasons
support.follows: All reasoning beings share a single soul.

claims.changed: Marcus says soul, reason and intellectual soul by turns. The fused claim says “reason” throughout.

claims.t: We are made for one another and for one common work, and that shared life is our own good.
claims.shared: Each says that a reasonable being is directed toward its own kind, whether by its making (7.10, 9.21, 5.15) or by its nature (9.7). 5.15 and 9.7 both say the direction is toward one another, and 5.15 and 7.10 both call it its own good.

support.quote: all made and prepared for one common operation
gives: for one common work
We are made
support.follows: All are made and prepared for one shared work.

support.quote: As thou thyself, whoever thou art, were made for the perfection and consummation, being a member of it, of a common society
gives: We are made
support.follows: I was made to complete a shared society, as one of its members.

support.quote: Whatsoever therefore is partaker of that reasonable common nature, naturally doth as much and more long after his own kind.
gives: for one another
support.follows: Whatever shares in reason is naturally drawn to others who share in it.

support.quote: Society therefore is the proper good of a rational creature.
gives: that shared life is our own good
support.follows: Living with others is what is good for a reasoning being.

support.quote: For that we are made for society, it hath long since been demonstrated.
gives: We are made
support.follows: It has already been shown that we are made for society.

support.quote: those things that are best, are made one for another? And those things that have souls, are better than those that have none? and of those that have, those best that have rational souls?
gives: We are made
for one another
support.note: Asked as questions no one can answer with no: the best things are made for one another, and the best are those with reasoning souls.
support.follows: The best things are made for one another, and the best of all are those with reasoning souls.

support.quote: as doing good to thyself, when thou dost good unto others
gives: our own good
support.note: The good of the other and my own are the same act.
support.follows: When I do good to others, I do good to myself.

claims.t: So each thing I do should aim at the common good, directly or at a distance, and holding to that one aim is what makes me one person.
claims.shared: Two passages draw the same consequence from membership: the aim of action is common. 11.19 adds what the single aim does for the one who holds it.

support.quote: so must every action of thine tend to the perfection and consummation of a life that is truly sociable
gives: each thing I do should aim at the common good
support.follows: Every action of mine should help make shared life complete.

support.quote: What action soever of thine therefore that either immediately or afar off, hath not reference to the common good, that is an exorbitant and disorderly action
gives: directly or at a distance
aim at the common good
support.follows: An action with no connection to the common good is out of order, even when the connection would only be distant.

support.quote: so must the end also that we propose unto ourselves, be common and sociable
gives: aim at the common good
support.follows: The goal I set for myself should be a common one.

support.quote: he that doth direct all his own private motions and purposes to that end, all his actions will be agreeable and uniform; and by that means will be still the same man
gives: holding to that one aim is what makes me one person
support.follows: A person who directs all his purposes to that one end acts consistently and stays the same person.

claims.t: When I hate someone, wrong them, or resent what happens, I cut myself off, and not from that one thing only but from the whole.
claims.shared: Three pictures of severing (a branch, a limb, a faction). In each the person does it to himself, and in each the cut is from the whole.

support.quote: he that hates and is averse, cuts himself off from his neighbour
gives: When I hate someone
I cut myself off
support.follows: Hatred and aversion are how a person cuts himself off from a neighbour.

support.quote: and knows not that at the same time he divides himself from the whole body, or corporation
gives: from the whole
support.follows: In the same act, and without knowing it, he separates himself from the whole body of people.

support.quote: If ever thou sawest either a hand, or a foot, or a head lying by itself, in some place or other, as cut off from the rest of the body, such must thou conceive him to make himself, as much as in him lieth, that either is offended with anything that is happened
gives: resent what happens
support.note: 8.32 counts resentment of events as a cut too.
support.follows: A person who resents anything that has happened makes himself, as far as he can, like a hand or foot cut off from the body.

support.quote: or that commits anything against the natural law of mutual correspondence, and society among men
gives: wrong them
support.follows: Acting against the natural law of fellowship among people is counted as the same kind of act.

support.quote: he needed not, except he would himself, have divided himself from the whole
gives: I cut myself off
from the whole
support.follows: A person is divided from the whole only by his own will.

support.quote: as one among the people who from such and such a consent and unity, should factiously divide and separate himself
gives: I cut myself off
support.follows: It is like a man who breaks away from a united people to form a faction.

claims.t: Having cut myself off, I can grow back into the whole, because nature is stronger than my leaving.
claims.shared: Two passages say the return is possible in almost the same words. 9.7 says something else: those who flee their nature are caught by it. Joining the two with “because” is the editor’s step.

support.quote: once cut off we may grow together and become part of the whole again
gives: I can grow back into the whole
support.follows: Once cut off, we can grow together again and be part of the whole again.

support.quote: if he would himself, he might return, and grow together again
gives: I can grow back
support.follows: Return is possible if the person wants it.

support.quote: But though they fly from nature, yet are they stopt in their course, and apprehended.
gives: nature is stronger than my leaving
support.follows: Reasoning beings cannot finally escape their nature; it catches up with them.

claims.changed: Both 11.7 and 8.32 credit the return to God. The fused claim credits nature, following 9.7.

inferences.why: No passage gives this reason: 11.7 and 8.32 credit the return to God, and 9.7 speaks of flight from nature, not of return.

single.label: A practice
single.t: I shall often say to myself: I am a member, and not merely a part.
single.quote: use thyself often to say to thyself, I am μέλος, or a member of the mass and body of reasonable substances
single.why: Only 7.10 gives an exercise. It is kept as the article’s practice.
single.follows: I should often tell myself that I am a member of this body.

single.label: A warning
single.t: The more often I cut myself off, the harder the return.
single.quote: But if this happen often the misery is that the further a man is run in this division, the harder he is to be reunited and restored again
single.why: Only 11.7 says the return gets harder. One witness, so it is not fused into claim 5.
single.follows: Each repeated separation makes reunion harder.

decisions: Reads body, city, sunlight and soul as four pictures of one claim. Marcus sets sunlight beside soul himself (12.23, 9.7); body and city he never lines up with them.
Joins the return (11.7, 8.32) to 9.7 with “because”. Marcus states the return and credits it to God; he does not derive it.
Says “nature” where two of the three passages behind claim 5 say God.
articles.limit: Nine of the ten passages feed the article. That is also a risk: fusing smooths over differences. 4.4 argues for the unity step by step, and 9.7 argues from the elements; the article states the unity and keeps neither argument. Nine of the 22 components of its claims rest on two or more passages; the other thirteen are one passage’s words.

aside.8.52: A wish to share one mind as we share one air. Close to claim 1, but a wish and not a statement.

statement.t: I am a member of one body of reasoning beings, made for a shared life with them.

parts.words: made for a shared life with them

statement.kind: Many pictures, one claim; then its consequences
statement.form: The statement gathers claims 1 and 2. Claim 1 is fused from four passages that use different pictures: body, city, sunlight, soul; claim 2 from four that say what we are made for. Claims 3 and 4 are what Marcus draws from it; the “because” of claim 5 is the editor’s.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section considers that reasoning beings might not be one. The doubt is taken up under Article 3.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the two central claims gain a second author, the body picture gains an arch beside it, and the article gains a concrete act, a second exercise and a caution about crowds: I may step back from them, but I must not hate them. He disputes none of Marcus’s claims here.
seneca.statement: The statement stands. With Seneca it gains the arch: we do not only belong together, we hold one another up.

items.quote: we are the parts of one great body
gives: as limbs share one body
items.follows: We are all parts of one great body.
items.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “We” is gods and humans together: all that you see is one.

items.quote: Nature produced us related to one another, since she created us from the same source and to the same end. She engendered in us mutual affection, and made us prone to friendships.
gives: We are made
for one another
items.follows: Nature made us kin, from one source and for one end, and gave us affection for one another.
items.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “Us” is all human beings; “she” is Nature.

items.quote: no one can live happily who has regard to himself alone and transforms everything into a question of his own utility; you must live for your neighbour, if you would live for yourself
gives: that shared life is our own good
items.follows: No one lives happily for himself alone; to live for myself I have to live for another.
items.context: Opens on friendship (a friend’s interest is mine), then widens to all fellow men in 48.3. “Your neighbour” is any other person, the friend first.

items.label: why
items.t: We hold one another up as the stones of an arch do: without that support the arch falls.
items.why: Marcus has body, city, sunlight and soul. The arch adds something none of them states: that the whole stands only because its parts hold one another up.

support.quote: Our relations with one another are like a stone arch, which would collapse if the stones did not mutually support each other
support.follows: Human fellowship stands the way a stone arch does: only because its parts support one another.
support.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “Our relations with one another” is human fellowship as a whole, not one friendship.

items.label: action
items.t: My hands should be ready for anyone who needs help.
items.why: Marcus’s claim says to aim at the common good. Seneca names what that looks like when someone is in front of me.

support.quote: Through her orders, let our hands be ready for all that needs to be helped
support.follows: By Nature’s order we should be ready to help whatever needs help.
support.context: The practical close of Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people. “Her” is Nature; those to be helped are people in need, like the shipwrecked and the starving just named.

items.label: practice
items.t: I shall keep one line in my heart and on my lips: I am human, and nothing human is foreign to me.
items.why: A second exercise beside Marcus’s own. The line is from the playwright Terence; Seneca quotes it as something to repeat.

support.quote: Let this verse be in your heart and on your lips: I am a man; and nothing in man’s lot Do I deem foreign to me.
support.follows: I should keep ready a line that says nothing human is foreign to me.
support.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “This verse” is a line of Terence, unnamed here, that Lucilius is told to keep ready.

items.label: breaks
items.t: I should not hate the many for being unlike me. I may withdraw into myself as far as I can, and keep the company that makes me better and that I can make better.
items.why: Marcus says that hating cuts me off. Seneca, writing about crowds that unsettle a character not yet firm, forbids the hatred and still advises stepping back. He does not speak of cutting off, so this is an addition, not a dispute.

support.quote: nor should you hate the many because they are unlike you. Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can. Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve.
support.follows: I should not hate the crowd for being unlike me; I should withdraw into myself as far as I can and keep company that improves me and that I can improve.
support.context: A letter on avoiding crowds, which unsettle a character not yet firm. “The many” is the crowd, as at the games; “withdraw” is from it, not from everyone.

amend.t: , each of us holding the others up as the stones of an arch do

rejected.why: “we are his members”: members of God, in an argument that the soul is divine; not about one another
“parts and members of a single whole” are the virtues inside one soul
one soul, many virtues: a logic puzzle about virtue, not about people
an army or senate as a body of separate members: a preface to an argument about renown
the wise man’s good is common: his wisdom helps others too; an argument that he cannot be harmed
fellowship among men torn by avarice: a history of early mankind, not what I do
“this whole world is my country”: about travel and place, not fellow citizens
“born to love all men”: a premise in an argument about renown; 95.52 says it directly
nature draws men to each other: on friendship; 95.52 already says it
the wise man’s good stays within himself: a real limit on claim 2, proposed to the owner, not added
fellowship with all men helps friendship: continues 48.2, which is in use
reason as a portion of the divine spirit: argues that goods are equal, not that we share reason
our reason derives from divine reason: about the parts of the soul
the sun unimpaired by obstacles: a picture of virtue, not of one light shared
peace and liberty belong whole to each: thanks owed to rulers, not fellowship
wrongdoing poisons the doer: about ingratitude; self-harm, not being cut off
every animal looks out for itself first: describes instinct, gives no rule for action
grafting a vine: about a pupil too spoiled to take teaching, not a return to fellowship
avoid the many, the few, the one: solitude is safe only for the good; 7.8 is the fuller text
the unready are better in any company than alone: the reverse of 7.8, kept as a note on his consistency
he withdrew to write for later generations: confirms that his stepping back is no break with people

articles.title: The work that belongs to me

claims.t: Among other people, I mean well by my own kind and aim at the common good. This comes first.
claims.shared: All three lists have this item. 7.30 calls it chief and 8.25 names it first; 8.6 names it second, after judgment. Only 7.30 ranks it.

support.quote: That therefore which is chief in every man's constitution, is, that he intend the common good.
gives: aim at the common good
This comes first
support.follows: The most important thing in a human being is to aim at the common good.

support.quote: That which is most proper unto a man, is, first, to be kindly affected towards them that are of the same kind and nature as he is himself
gives: mean well by my own kind
support.follows: What is most proper to a human being is, first, goodwill toward those of his own kind.

support.quote: when in all its motions and resolutions it takes its level at the common good only
gives: aim at the common good
support.follows: A reasoning nature does well when all its impulses aim only at the common good.

support.quote: as we are bound to do them good, and to bear with them
gives: mean well by my own kind
support.follows: We are bound to do good to other people and to be patient with them.

claims.t: With my body, I do not let its urges rule me. Reason was made to be in charge of the body.
claims.shared: Two of the three lists have the item about not yielding. 8.6 has none about the body; it speaks of desire in general. That reason was made to command the body is said by 7.30 alone.

support.quote: The second is, that he yield not to any lusts and motions of the flesh.
gives: I do not let its urges rule me
support.follows: A human being should not give in to bodily urges.

support.quote: to contemn all sensual motions and appetites
gives: I do not let its urges rule me
support.follows: It is proper to a human being to look down on bodily urges and appetites.

support.quote: For by nature she was ordained to command all in the body.
gives: Reason was made to be in charge of the body
support.follows: Reason is by nature the part that commands the body.

support.quote: But one whereby pleasure and voluptuousness may be resisted and opposed, I see: continence.
support.note: Names the virtue that does this work.
support.follows: Self-restraint is the virtue that resists pleasure.
gives: I do not let its urges rule me

claims.t: In my judgments I take care: I do not accept what is false or uncertain, and I do not judge in a hurry.
claims.shared: All three lists have this item. 8.6 puts it first and 7.30 last.

support.quote: The third thing proper to man by his constitution, is, to avoid all rashness and precipitancy; and not to be subject to error.
gives: I do not judge in a hurry
I do not accept what is false or uncertain
support.follows: A human being should avoid haste in judging and should not be deceived.

support.quote: A reasonable nature doth then speed, when first in matter of fancies and imaginations, it gives no consent to that which is either false uncertain
gives: I do not accept what is false or uncertain
support.follows: A reasoning nature does well when it does not agree to anything false or uncertain.

support.quote: to discern rightly all plausible fancies and imaginations
gives: I take care
support.follows: It is proper to a human being to judge persuasive impressions correctly.

support.quote: For justice cannot be preserved, if either we settle our minds and affections upon worldly things; or be apt to be deceived, or rash, and inconstant.
gives: I do not judge in a hurry
I do not accept what is false or uncertain
support.note: Not from a list of what is proper to man: said of what destroys justice.
support.follows: Justice cannot be kept by someone who is attached to worldly things, or is easily deceived, hasty or changeable.

claims.t: Doing this work is living according to my own nature. That is why it cannot harm me, and why doing it makes me content.
claims.shared: Joy, content and happiness are three words in three passages for one thing: doing my proper work is its own reward. Two passages say the work is according to nature. Only 6.31 says it cannot harm.

support.quote: The true joy of a man, is to do that which properly belongs unto a man.
gives: doing it makes me content
support.follows: A human being’s real joy is in doing what belongs to a human being.

support.quote: Every particular nature hath content, when in its own proper course it speeds.
gives: doing it makes me content
support.follows: Every nature is content when it proceeds along its own course.

support.quote: So a man as long as he doth that which is proper unto a man, his labour cannot be against nature
gives: living according to my own nature
support.follows: Work that is proper to a human being cannot be against nature.

support.quote: and if it be not against nature, then neither is it hurtful unto him
gives: it cannot harm me
support.follows: What is not against nature does not harm the one who does it.

support.quote: and she hath her end, and by consequent her happiness
gives: doing it makes me content
support.follows: The mind then has its end, and with that its happiness.

support.quote: To a reasonable creature, the same action is both according to nature, and according to reason.
support.note: Why work done by reason counts as natural.
support.follows: For a reasoning being, acting by reason and acting by nature are the same.
gives: living according to my own nature

claims.t: The work is the act itself, not its result and not what I feel. And when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action.
claims.shared: Two passages place the work in the acting itself; only 5.14 rules out the result, and only 9.14 rules out what I feel. Three more, in three images, say an obstacle is turned into the next object of action.

support.quote: Reason, and rational power, are faculties which content themselves with themselves, and their own proper operations.
gives: The work is the act itself
support.follows: Reason needs nothing beyond itself and its own activity.

support.quote: The final ends and consummations of actions are nothing at all to a man's nature.
gives: not its result
support.follows: How an action finally turns out is not part of what a human being is.

support.quote: so neither doth the true good or evil of a reasonable charitable man consist in passion, but in operation and action
gives: The work is the act itself
not what I feel
support.follows: A person’s good and bad lie in what he does, not in what he feels.

support.quote: For by these the mind doth turn and convert any impediment whatsoever, to be her aim and purpose.
gives: when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action
support.follows: The mind can turn any obstacle into its new aim.

support.quote: so that whatsoever it is that falls out contrary to its first intentions, even that afterwards it makes its proper object
gives: when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action
support.follows: When something goes against its first plan, the mind takes that very thing as its next object.

support.quote: what crosses and impediments soever it meets with in the course of this mortal life, it may use them as fit and proper objects, to the furtherance of whatsoever it intended
gives: when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action
support.follows: A reasoning being can use whatever obstacles it meets as material for what it set out to do.

single.label: Only in one list
single.t: I may add a fourth work: to contemplate the nature of the universe.
single.quote: to contemplate the nature of the universe
single.why: Neither of the other two lists has it, so it is not fused. Article 4 takes it up.
single.follows: Contemplating the nature of the universe is also proper to a human being.

single.label: Only in one list
single.t: And I may welcome gladly whatever the common nature deals out.
single.quote: when it willingly and gladly embraceth, whatsoever is dealt and appointed unto it by the common nature
single.why: Only 8.6 puts this in the list. It is the whole subject of Article 3.
single.follows: A reasoning nature does well when it gladly accepts what nature assigns it.

single.label: A direction
single.t: To these I shall apply my mind and go straight on, without distraction about other things.
single.quote: To these things then, let the mind apply herself and go straight on, without any distraction about other things
single.why: Only 7.30 turns the list into an instruction.
single.follows: The mind should keep to these three things and not be distracted by others.

decisions: Treats the three lists as versions of one list. Marcus never says they are the same list.

Names the three places “other people, my body, my judgments”, and sums them up as “letting reason lead”. The names and the summary are the editor’s: 7.30 says reason commands the body and 7.8 that acting by reason is acting by nature; neither says it of other people or of judging.
Joins the passages about outcomes with those about obstacles in claim 5, as two sides of one point.
articles.limit: The alignment is clean for two of the three items. The item about the body is missing from 8.6, and each list has something the others lack. Those leftovers are shown under “said once”. Inside the claims, three things rest on one passage each: that the common good comes first (7.30), that reason was made to command the body (7.30), and that proper work cannot harm (6.31).

aside.11.18: The elements keep their place; the mind that resents does not. An argument for submission, nearer to Article 3.
aside.9.1: A long passage that calls injustice, lying and pleasure-seeking impious. It argues for the same three works from piety, a ground the article does not use.
aside.7.42: What offers nothing to reason or to charity is beneath the reasonable faculty. A test for objects, not a description of the work.

statement.t: My work is to let reason lead in how I treat other people, in how I handle my body, and in how I judge.
statement.form: Three passages (7.30, 8.25 and 8.6) each list what is proper to a human being, in different words and at different lengths. The statement and the three claims under “In action” come from aligning those lists item by item.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what remains if reason is not what a human being is for.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author and Practice gains a way to stay my own master amid business. To the claim about the body he adds that it may still be indulged somewhat.
seneca.statement: The statement stands. Seneca names its ground outright: reason is what is peculiar to a human being.

items.quote: I am naturally born to love all men
gives: mean well by my own kind
items.follows: I am born to love all human beings.
items.context: Seneca argues that praise from good men is a good for the man praised; “I” is that good man, glad of it because he loves all people by nature.

items.quote: I do not maintain that the body is not to be indulged at all; but I maintain that we must not be slaves to it
gives: I do not let its urges rule me
items.follows: The body may be indulged somewhat, but we must not be its slaves.
items.context: On our love of the body, which we must guard; “it” is the body, and the slavery he describes is living for it and fearing on its behalf.

items.quote: our alliance shall nevertheless not be one of equality; the soul shall bring all quarrels before its own tribunal
gives: Reason was made to be in charge of the body
items.follows: While soul and body are joined they are not equals: the soul judges every dispute between them.
items.context: Seneca refuses to live as his body’s chattel; “our alliance” is the soul’s with the body while they are bound together. A resolve, not a law of nature.

items.quote: And what is it which this reason demands of him? The easiest thing in the world,—to live in accordance with his own nature
gives: living according to my own nature
items.follows: What reason asks of a human being is to live by his own nature.
items.context: Seneca has just said a man’s own good is reason perfected in the soul; “his own nature” is the nature of man as a reasoning animal.

items.quote: What then is peculiar to man? Reason. When this is right and has reached perfection, man’s felicity is complete.
gives: doing it makes me content
items.follows: Reason is what is peculiar to a human being; when it is right and perfected, his happiness is complete.
items.context: Each thing is judged by the good that is its own, as a stag by speed; “this” is reason, and he speaks of reason made perfect, not of work under way.

items.quote: the wise man regards the reason for all his actions, but not the results. The beginning is in our own power; fortune decides the issue
gives: not its result
items.follows: The wise man looks to the reasons for what he does, not to how it turns out: the start is ours, the outcome is fortune’s.
items.context: Seneca has admitted that a careful life cannot guarantee safety; “the results” are how the wise man’s actions turn out, which fortune decides.

items.quote: Because of his poverty he is prevented from showing how the State should be handled; but he teaches, none the less, how poverty should be handled.
gives: when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action
items.follows: Kept by poverty from showing how a state should be handled, the wise man shows how poverty should be handled.
items.context: Seneca answers that hardship cannot stop the wise man as a storm stops a pilot; “he” is the wise man, whom poverty keeps out of public life.

items.label: practice
items.t: I lend myself to my affairs; I do not hand myself over to them.
items.why: Marcus says to keep to the three things and not be distracted. Seneca, writing about keeping time for study, says how he stays his own master amid business.

support.quote: I do not surrender myself to my affairs, but loan myself to them
support.follows: I can take part in business without giving myself up to it.
support.context: Seneca denies that business keeps anyone from study; “my affairs” are his engagements, and what he keeps back is his time and his own thoughts.

articles.title: What happens to me

claims.role: It comes from one chain of causes
claims.t: What happens to me is not chance. All things are linked together, and it comes from a chain of causes, the same that produced me.
claims.shared: Five passages use one family of words: connection, concatenation, coherence, linked, correspondence. Two (7.6, 4.36) say that things hold together. Three (10.5, 5.8, 1.17) say that what happens comes through that holding. Only 10.5 says the same causes produced me, and only 1.17 speaks of chance.

support.quote: For by the same coherence of causes, by which thy substance from all eternity was appointed to be, was also whatsoever should happen unto it, destinated and appointed.
gives: it comes from a chain of causes
the same that produced me
support.follows: The causes that produced me also produced everything that happens to me.

support.quote: from the very beginning by the series and connection of the first causes, it hath ever had a reference unto thee
gives: it comes from a chain of causes
support.follows: What happens to me was connected to me from the beginning through the chain of causes.

support.quote: All things are linked and knitted together, and the knot is sacred
gives: All things are linked together
support.follows: Everything is connected to everything else.

support.quote: those things that are commonly said to happen by fortune, even those must be conceived to have dependence from nature, or from that first and general connection, and concatenation of all those things
gives: is not chance
chain of causes
support.follows: Even what is said to happen by chance depends on nature, or on one connected chain of things.

support.quote: There is then to be seen in the things of the world, not a bare succession, but an admirable correspondence and affinity.
gives: All things are linked together
support.follows: The things of the world do not merely follow one another; they correspond and belong together.

claims.changed: “Not a random blow from outside” is gone: no passage says “from outside”, and 4.36 sets its order against a bare sequence, not against chance. 7.6 now backs “linked together”, which it says, and no longer “chain of causes”, which it does not.

claims.t: It serves the whole of which I am a part. What serves the whole is good for every part, and a part has no reason to complain of it.
claims.shared: Three passages say that what happens is useful to the whole, and two that I am a part of it. Two go on to the part, and each says a different thing: 1.17 that what the whole needs is good for every part, 9.38 that a part has no reason to complain of it. They share the subject, not the conclusion.

support.quote: Whatsoever in any kind doth happen to any one, is expedient to the whole.
gives: It serves the whole
support.follows: What happens to any individual is useful to the whole.

support.quote: For this whatsoever it be, should not have been produced, had it not conduced to the good of the universe.
gives: It serves the whole
support.follows: Nothing would have happened unless it helped the good of the universe.

support.quote: whatsoever it is that is, is both necessary, and conducing to the whole (part of which thou art)
gives: It serves the whole
of which I am a part
support.follows: Whatever exists is necessary and helps the whole, and I am part of that whole.

support.quote: whatsoever it is that is requisite and necessary for the preservation of the general, must of necessity for every particular nature, be good and behoveful
gives: What serves the whole is good for every part
support.follows: Whatever is needed to preserve the whole is good and useful for every part of it.

support.quote: all things by the providence of reason happen unto every particular, as a part of one general body; and then it is against reason that a part should complain of anything that happens for the good of the whole
gives: of which I am a part
What serves the whole
a part has no reason to complain of it
support.follows: If things happen to each of us as a part of one body, a part has no reason to complain of what happens for the good of the whole.

claims.changed: Was “what serves the whole is not bad for the part”, a middle wording that neither passage says: 1.17 says “good”, and 9.38 speaks of complaining, not of harm. Each now backs its own words.

claims.t: So I shall accept it, and more than accept it: fit myself to it and be glad of it, as I take a harsh prescription for the sake of health.
claims.shared: Four passages give the same instruction with rising warmth: accept, fit yourself, embrace, be pleased. Only 5.8 has the physician. “So” is Marcus’s own step in 5.8 (“therefore”, “then”). “And more than accept it” is the editor’s link and rests on no quote.

support.quote: These therefore let us accept of in like manner, as we do those that are prescribed unto us our physicians. For them also in themselves shall We find to contain many harsh things, but we nevertheless, in hope of health, and recovery, accept of them.
gives: as I take a harsh prescription for the sake of health
So I shall accept it
support.follows: I should accept what happens as I accept a doctor’s prescription: harsh in itself, and taken in hope of health.

support.quote: Accept then, and be pleased with whatsoever doth happen, though otherwise harsh and un-pleasing
gives: be glad of it
So I shall accept it
support.follows: I should accept what happens and be glad of it, even when it is harsh.

support.quote: Fit and accommodate thyself to that estate and to those occurrences, which by the destinies have been annexed unto thee
gives: fit myself to it
support.follows: I should adapt myself to the circumstances I have been given.

support.quote: to like and embrace all things that happen and are destinated unto him
gives: be glad of it
support.follows: The stance named here is to like and welcome everything that happens and is destined for me.
support.note: In 3.17 this is part of what belongs to a good man alone; that part of the sentence lies outside the quote.

support.quote: willing of himself without any compulsion to fit and accommodate himself to his proper lot and portion
gives: fit myself to it
support.follows: I should fit myself to my own lot willingly, without being forced.

support.quote: those things which in consequence and coherence of this general deliberation happen unto me in particular, I am bound to embrace and accept of
gives: So I shall accept it
support.follows: I am bound to welcome and accept what happens to me as a consequence of the general plan.

claims.t: None of it is unusual. Sickness, death and slander are as ordinary as roses in spring.
claims.shared: Two passages make what happens familiar and recurring.

support.quote: Whatsoever doth happen in the world, is, in the course of nature, as usual and ordinary as a rose in the spring, and fruit in summer.
gives: as ordinary as roses in spring
None of it is unusual
support.follows: Everything that happens is as ordinary as the seasons.

support.quote: Of the same nature is sickness and death; slander, and lying in wait
gives: Sickness, death and slander
support.follows: Sickness, death, slander and treachery are ordinary in the same way.

support.quote: Up and down, from one age to another, go the ordinary things of the world; being still the same.
gives: None of it is unusual
support.follows: The same ordinary things recur in every age.

claims.t: And if nothing governs the world, I still have a reason of my own, and can govern what is mine with it.
claims.shared: Four passages grant the other case, that nothing governs. Three end the same way, with my own reason left to govern what is mine (9.26, 12.11, 6.39). 9.38 ends only with “why trouble yourself?”. This is the most repeated move in the section.

support.quote: or if all things go by chance and fortune, yet mayest thou use thine own providence in those things that concern thee properly; and then art thou well
gives: And if nothing governs the world
can govern what is mine with it
support.follows: Even if everything is chance, I can still use my own foresight in what concerns me.

support.quote: If all be a mere confusion without any moderator, or governor, then hast thou reason to congratulate thyself; that in such a general flood of confusion thou thyself hast obtained a reasonable faculty, whereby thou mayest govern thine own life and actions
gives: And if nothing governs the world
I still have a reason of my own
can govern what is mine with it
support.follows: Even in a world without order, I have reason and can govern my life with it.

support.quote: if so be that they have not indeed either in general, or particular deliberated of any of those things, that happen unto us in this world; yet God be thanked, that of those things that concern myself, it is lawful for me to deliberate myself
gives: And if nothing governs the world
can govern what is mine with it
support.follows: Even if the gods plan nothing, I may still deliberate about my own affairs.

support.quote: if, according to Epicurus, atoms be the cause of all things and that life be nothing else but an accidentary confusion of things, and death nothing else, but a mere dispersion and so of all other things: what doest thou trouble thyself for?
support.note: On the atomist case Marcus does not say here that reason remains, only that there is nothing to be troubled about.
support.follows: If everything is only atoms, there is nothing for me to be troubled about.
gives: And if nothing governs the world

single.label: A warning
single.t: Each time I am displeased with what happens, I cut something away from the whole, as far as lies in me.
single.quote: For the whole (because whole, therefore entire and perfect) is maimed, and mutilated, if thou shalt cut off anything at all, whereby the coherence, and contiguity as of parts, so of causes, is maintained and preserved. Of which certain it is, that thou doest (as much as lieth in thee) cut off, and in some sort violently take somewhat away, as often as thou art displeased with anything that happeneth
single.why: One witness in this section. 8.32, in the section behind Article 1, says the same with a severed limb.
single.follows: Each time I am displeased with what happens I cut something off from the whole, as far as I am able.

single.label: An addition
single.t: And I shall love the people fate has given me to live with, and love them truly.
single.quote: and love those men whom thy fate it is to live with; but love them truly
single.why: Only 6.35 turns acceptance toward people. It is kept apart for a later article.
single.follows: I should truly love the people it is my fate to live with.

decisions: Presents the section as one argument by cases. Marcus gives the cases in four passages and never the whole chain in one place.

Keeps apart the two things said about the part: 1.17 says what the whole needs is good for every part, 9.38 that a part has no reason to complain. An earlier draft merged them into “not bad for the part”, which neither says.

Records no editor’s inference. The one “so”, in the claim under In action, is Marcus’s own: 5.8 gives the chain of causes and the good of the whole as its two reasons for being pleased with what happens.
Says nothing about acting to change what can be changed. That is Article 2. Accepting what has happened is not an instruction to do nothing.
articles.limit: Claims 1 to 4 hold only in the first case. If you do not think the world is governed, the article reduces to claim 5, and Marcus would not object: he says so himself. That what serves the whole is good for me has one witness here (1.17); Article 6 returns to it from its own passages.

aside.7.22: A list of reminders about order, death, pain and praise. Too many subjects to fuse with anything here.
aside.3.12: Questions to ask of any impression, tracing each thing to God, fate or a neighbour. An exercise in examining impressions, nearer to judgment than to accepting what happens.
aside.4.8: What happens, happens justly. A stronger claim than claim 2, and only this passage makes it.

statement.t: Whatever happens to me, I accept it and do not complain.
statement.kind: An argument by cases, found four times
statement.form: This is an argument by cases, and Marcus makes it four times in this section. “Why” holds the first case, that the world is governed. “If I doubt it” holds the second. “Do not complain” gathers three wordings: complain (9.38), be displeased (5.8), and, on the second case, trouble yourself (9.38).

empty.practice: No passage used in this article gives an exercise. The physician of 5.8 is a comparison, not something to do. 3.12, set aside, has one (to say of each thing where it comes from), but its subject is judging impressions.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca every claim gains a second author, the empty Practice label gets two exercises, “Why” gets a further argument, and “In action” gains what I may still prefer before a hardship comes. Nothing of Marcus’s is challenged.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement gains a preparation: I accept what happens, and I think ahead to it.

items.quote: Such affairs come by order, and not by accident.
gives: is not chance
items.follows: Troubles like these come by order, not by accident.
items.context: Seneca has just listed his own illness, sick slaves and lost income; “such affairs” are those troubles, which he calls inevitable.

items.quote: the very agencies which seem to bring harm are working for the preservation of the world
gives: It serves the whole
items.follows: What seems to harm me is working to preserve the world.
items.context: Seneca names the inner defence against Fortune: not chafing at what happens. “The very agencies” are the events that seem to harm us.

items.quote: I have trained myself not merely to obey God, but to agree with His decisions
gives: accept it, and more than accept it
items.follows: I can do more than obey what is decided: I can agree with it.
items.context: Said of the times “when everything seems to go hard”; “His decisions” are the illness and losses of 96.1, which Seneca says are decreed.

items.quote: It is to this law that our souls must adjust themselves, this they should follow, this they should obey. Whatever happens, assume that it was bound to happen, and do not be willing to rail at Nature.
gives: I shall accept it
fit myself to it
items.follows: My soul should adjust itself to nature’s law, take whatever happens as bound to happen, and not rail at it.
items.context: “This law” is nature’s order of changing seasons and opposites, which we cannot alter; “it” is whatever that order brings.

items.quote: None of these things is unusual or unexpected.
gives: None of it is unusual
items.follows: Setbacks like these are neither unusual nor unexpected.
items.context: “These things” are Lucilius’s slaves running away; Seneca widens it at once to every knock on life’s journey.

items.quote: whether Chance drives and tosses human affairs without method, philosophy ought to be our defence
gives: And if nothing governs the world
items.follows: Even if chance drives everything, philosophy is still my defence.
items.context: Seneca answers the objection that philosophy is useless if fate, God or chance rules: in each case we need it. “Chance” is the third case.

items.label: why
items.t: And refusing does not spare me: fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling.
items.why: Marcus argues from the good of the whole. This argues that I go either way. Marcus only touches it, in 12.11 (“why doest thou resist?”), which this article uses for something else. Seneca gives the line as Cleanthes’s, in his own Latin.

support.quote: the willing soul Fate leads, but the unwilling drags along
support.follows: Fate takes me along whether I am willing or not.
support.context: The last line of Cleanthes’s prayer to Jupiter, which Seneca puts into Latin to close a letter on following nature’s law; the soul is anyone’s.
gives: fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling

items.label: practice
items.t: I shall think ahead to everything that can happen, not only to what usually does, so that the blow is lighter when it comes.
items.why: The passages used here give no exercise. Seneca gives this one in three letters. He also warns against overdoing it: in Ep. 13.10 he says not to run out to meet a suffering that has not come.

support.quote: Our minds should be sent forward in advance to meet all problems, and we should consider, not what is wont to happen, but what can happen.
support.follows: I should think ahead to what can happen, not only to what usually happens.
gives: think ahead to everything that can happen, not only to what usually does
support.context: Written after fire destroyed Lyons and shook his friend Liberalis; “all problems” are whatever Fortune can do, since the unexpected weighs heaviest.

support.quote: If an evil has been pondered beforehand, the blow is gentle when it comes.
support.follows: A misfortune I have already thought about hits less hard.
gives: the blow is lighter when it comes
support.context: Follows a picture of the man who hears of chains and exile calmly; “an evil” is any such threatened hardship, new only to the unprepared.

support.quote: That which has been long expected comes more gently.
support.follows: What I have long expected is easier when it arrives.
gives: the blow is lighter when it comes
support.context: The closing advice of a letter on illness: keep Fortune’s whole power before your eyes. “That which” is any blow she may strike.

items.label: practice
items.t: For a set number of days I shall live on the plainest food and clothing, and ask myself: is this what I was afraid of?
items.why: A second exercise, done with the body and not only in thought. It rehearses a loss before it comes; that is how it bears on accepting what happens.

support.quote: Set aside a certain number of days, during which you shall be content with the scantiest and cheapest fare, with coarse and rough dress, saying to yourself the while: “Is this the condition that I feared?”
support.follows: I should spend set days living poorly and ask myself whether this is what I feared.
support.context: A lesson for the Saturnalia: rehearse poverty while Fortune is kind, so that she cannot catch me off guard. “The condition” is being poor.

items.label: doubt
items.t: In that case my stance changes too: a god I follow gladly, but chance I endure, and defy.
items.why: Marcus says only that I can still govern myself. Seneca adds how to stand toward a world run by chance.

support.quote: She will encourage us to obey God cheerfully, but Fortune defiantly; she will teach us to follow God and endure Chance.
support.follows: Philosophy teaches me to obey a god cheerfully, and to endure chance and defy it.
support.context: “She” is philosophy, our defence whether fate, God or chance rules; the sentence sets how to stand toward God against how to stand toward Fortune.

items.label: action
items.t: I need not wish for the hardship. I may prefer to be spared it; what I want, if it must be borne, is to bear it with courage.
items.why: Marcus says to be glad of what comes; he does not say what I may wish beforehand. Seneca does. It is not a disagreement: Seneca too is pleased with what has come (Ep. 96.2, 74.20).

support.quote: I should prefer to be free from torture; but if the time comes when it must be endured, I shall desire that I may conduct myself therein with bravery, honour, and courage.
gives: I may prefer to be spared it; what I want, if it must be borne, is to bear it with courage
support.follows: I may prefer not to be tortured; if it must be endured, what I desire is to bear it with courage.
support.context: Lucilius asked whether brave endurance of torture is a thing to pray for; Seneca answers that the bravery is desirable, not the torture.

support.quote: The conclusion is, not that hardships are desirable, but that virtue is desirable, which enables us patiently to endure hardships.
gives: I need not wish for the hardship
support.follows: Hardships are not what is desirable; the virtue that lets me endure them is.
support.context: The conclusion Seneca draws from torture, war and illness; “virtue” is brave conduct in them, the only thing there he calls desirable.

articles.title: The reason that governs the whole

claims.t: The world is one thing, ordered throughout, and all things in it are bound to one another.
claims.shared: Three passages call the world one (one living substance, a union, “one and general”), two call it ordered, and two say that all things in it are tied together. 4.22 and 6.8 each put order as one of two cases.
claims.changed: 4.33 says more: that each thing helps to cause the others. The claim keeps what 4.22 also says, that all things are bound together; the causing is kept in the practice claim.

support.quote: the world as being but one living substance, and having but one soul
gives: The world is one thing
support.follows: The world is one living thing with one soul.

support.quote: can at one time subsist, and coexist in that both one and general, which we call the world
gives: The world is one thing
support.follows: Everything that happens can exist together in one world.

support.quote: or it is an union consisting of order, and administered by Providence
gives: The world is one thing
ordered throughout
support.note: The second of two cases. The first is under “said once”.
support.follows: The second possibility is that the world is a unity made of order and run by providence.

support.quote: Either this world is a κόσμος or comely piece, because all disposed and governed by certain order
gives: ordered throughout
support.note: The first of two cases. In the second he still calls the world a comely piece.
support.follows: One possibility is that the world is a well-made whole, because all in it is arranged and governed by order.

support.quote: and by what manner of connection and concatenation all things happen
gives: all things in it are bound to one another
support.follows: Everything that happens is linked to the rest, as in a chain.

support.quote: and yet all through diffused, and by natural sympathy, one to another united
gives: all things in it are bound to one another
support.follows: All things, though different, run through one another and are united by a natural sympathy.

claims.t: What governs it is reason, and everything that happens comes from it. It has no cause to do evil, it is for community, and even what is harmful follows from something good.
claims.shared: 6.1 and 5.24 both name a rational essence that governs the universe. 6.1, 6.33 and 7.44 all say that whatever happens comes from it. The last three points each rest on one passage.
claims.changed: 6.33 says “all hurtful things”; the claim no longer softens this to “what looks harmful”. 6.33 says “one beginning” and 7.44 “the nature of the universe”; the claim says “it” for both.

support.quote: That rational essence that doth govern it, hath in itself no cause to do evil.
gives: It has no cause to do evil
What governs it is reason
support.follows: The reason that governs the world has no motive to do evil.

support.quote: That rational essence by which the universe is governed, is for community and society
gives: it is for community
What governs it is reason
support.follows: The reason that governs the world aims at community.

support.quote: And all things are done and determined according to its will and prescript.
gives: everything that happens comes from it
support.follows: Everything is done and settled as the governing reason wills.

support.quote: And all things come from one beginning; either all severally and particularly deliberated and resolved upon, by the general ruler and governor of all; or all by necessary consequence.
gives: everything that happens comes from it
support.follows: All things come from one beginning: each decided by the ruler of all, or following by necessity.

support.quote: whatsoever it is, that is and happens in the world, is either but a consequent of that one and first deliberation
gives: everything that happens comes from it
support.note: The first of two cases. In the second the ruling part also takes thought for particular things.
support.follows: Whatever happens follows from the first deliberation of the universe, unless it is cared for in particular.

support.quote: and all hurtful things, are but (as the thorn and the mire) the necessary consequences of goodly fair things
gives: even what is harmful follows from something good
support.follows: Harmful things are necessary by-products of good and fair things.

claims.role: The same thing rules in me
claims.t: What rules in me is of one kind with it. It moves itself, and it turns everything else to its use. What I find in myself I can expect in the whole.
claims.shared: 5.18 and 6.7 both name a part of me that rules. 4.22 and 6.23 both argue from what is in me to what is in the whole. Only 5.18 says the two are of one kind.
claims.changed: 4.22 speaks of order in me and 6.23 of many things happening in me at once; the claim says “what I find in myself” for both. 5.18 says “all other things”, so “in me” is gone from the claim.

support.quote: and is of one kind and nature with that which we now spake of
gives: of one kind with it
support.follows: What is chief in me is of one kind and nature with what was just spoken of: what governs the world.

support.quote: For it is the very same, which being in thee, turneth all other things to its own use, and by whom also thy life is governed.
gives: it turns everything else to its use
What rules in me
support.follows: What is chief in me is the very same thing: it turns all else to its use and governs my life.

support.quote: The rational commanding part, as it alone can stir up and turn itself
gives: It moves itself
What rules in me
support.follows: The ruling part of me is the only thing that moves and directs itself.

support.quote: For is it possible that in thee there should be any beauty at all, and that in the whole world there should be nothing but disorder and confusion?
gives: What I find in myself I can expect in the whole
support.note: A likeness used as an argument: from order in me to order in the whole.
support.follows: If there is order in me, there cannot be only disorder in the world.

support.quote: Consider how many different things, whether they concern our bodies, or our souls, in a moment of time come to pass in every one of us, and so thou wilt not wonder
gives: What I find in myself I can expect in the whole
support.follows: So much happens in me at one moment that I need not wonder at the world holding all things at once.

claims.t: I shall make a habit of asking what causes each thing: the power at work in it, considered apart from its matter, and the one source of all things.
claims.shared: 4.33 and 10.26 both make it a standing habit (“ever consider”, “thou must use to behold”). 10.26, 9.23 and 4.33 all point at the cause and not the thing; 6.33 and 4.33 at the one origin.

support.quote: These things therefore that are so secretly and invisibly wrought and brought to pass, thou must use to behold and contemplate
gives: I shall make a habit
support.follows: I must make it my practice to look at what is brought about out of sight.

support.quote: Ever consider and think upon
gives: I shall make a habit
support.follows: This is something to consider and think about always.

support.quote: and not the things themselves only, but the power also by which they are effected
gives: the power at work
what causes each thing
support.follows: I should look at the power that produces things, and not only at the things.

support.quote: Go to the quality of the cause from which the effect doth proceed.
gives: what causes each thing
support.follows: I should go to the cause an effect comes from, and ask what kind of cause it is.

support.quote: and how all things that are, concur in the cause of one another's being
gives: what causes each thing
support.follows: Everything that exists helps cause everything else.

support.quote: Behold it by itself bare and naked, separated from all that is material.
gives: considered apart from its matter
support.follows: I should consider a cause by itself, apart from the material it works on.

support.quote: but consider in thy mind the true fountain of all
gives: the one source of all things
support.follows: I should keep in mind the true source of everything.

support.quote: are done by one general motion as it were, and deliberation of that one soul
gives: the one source of all things
support.follows: All things are done by one movement and one deliberation of the world's one soul.

claims.t: Thinking of the world as governed makes me calm, and I can be patient and trust what governs it.
claims.shared: 7.44 and 6.8 end on the same effect: tranquillity in one, quiet and patience in the other. Only 6.8 adds trust.
claims.changed: 7.44 says “often thought upon”; 6.8 puts it as a condition, “if the latter be”. The claim keeps the thought and the calm, which both have.

support.quote: This often thought upon, will much conduce to thy tranquillity.
gives: Thinking of the world as governed makes me calm
support.follows: Thinking about this often brings calm.

support.quote: But if the latter be, then am not I religious in vain; then will I be quiet and patient, and put my trust in Him, who is the Governor of all.
gives: Thinking of the world as governed makes me calm
I can be patient and trust what governs it
support.follows: If the world is ordered and governed, my worship is not wasted, and I will be quiet, patient and trusting.

single.label: An instruction
single.t: I shall honour what is chief and most powerful in the world, and in the same way what is chief in myself.
single.quote: Honour that which is chiefest and most powerful in the world, and that is it, which makes use of all things, and governs all things. So also in thyself; honour that which is chiefest, and most powerful
single.why: Only 5.18 says “honour”. It is the one place where the likeness becomes an instruction.
single.follows: I should honour what is most powerful in the world, and likewise what is most powerful in me.

single.label: A strong claim
single.t: Nothing can be hurt by it.
single.quote: neither can anything be hurt by it
single.why: Only 6.1 goes this far. It is kept apart so that the claim on what governs the world does not rest on it.
single.follows: Nothing can be harmed by the reason that governs the world.

single.label: A condition
single.t: If it takes thought for anything in particular, it is for those who reason.
single.quote: if so be that this ruling rational part of the world, takes any thought and care of things particular, they are surely his reasonable and principal creatures, that are the proper object of his particular care and providence
single.why: Only 7.44 speaks of care for particular beings, and only as a possibility. It stood in the claim on what governs the world without backing any of its words.
single.follows: If the governing reason cares for anything in particular, it cares for reasoning beings.

single.label: The other case
single.t: If the world were only confusion, why should I wish to stay in it?
single.quote: If the first, why should I desire to continue any longer in this fortuit confusion and commixtion?
single.why: Only here does Marcus say how the ungoverned case would feel. Article 3 carries his calmer answer.
single.follows: If the world were mere confusion, there would be no reason to want to remain in it.

decisions: Reads four descriptions of the world as one claim, and four of what governs it as another.

Makes the likeness between the whole and myself the centre of the article. Only 5.18 says the two are of one kind; 4.22 and 6.23 argue from myself to the whole, so the statement says “alike” and no more.
Keeps “nothing can be hurt by it” out of the fused claim, and keeps the particular care of 7.44 apart as well: Marcus puts it as a condition.
Joins 7.44 and 6.8 on calm as a claim of its own, under “In action”.
articles.limit: All twelve passages are used. This is a belief about the universe and the least argued of the five. Only 5.18 says that my reason and the world's are of one kind; the statement claims a likeness and no more. If you do not hold it, Articles 1 and 2 still stand on what human beings share, and Article 3 keeps its last claim.

statement.t: The reason that orders the world and the reason that guides me are alike.

parts.words: The reason that orders the world

statement.kind: A likeness between the whole and myself
statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 describe the world and claim 3 turns to me. 5.18 says the two are of one kind; 4.22 argues from the order in me to order in the whole. What both give is a likeness, so the statement says “alike”, and claim 3 keeps “of one kind” on 5.18 alone.

empty.breaks: No passage in this section describes losing sight of this, or recovering it.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author, the empty “When it breaks” gets its first item, “In action” says what worship of the governing power is enough, and “Why” gains a limit: its care may miss one person.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains what follows for worship: to imitate what orders the world, by being good, is enough.

items.quote: all that you behold, that which comprises both god and man, is one
gives: The world is one thing
items.follows: Everything there is, divine and human, is one.
items.context: Seneca's short rule for how to treat other people; “all that you behold” is the universe, gods and men together, of which we are parts.

items.quote: the divine reason also is set in supreme command over all things, and is itself subject to none
gives: What governs it is reason
items.follows: Divine reason commands everything and answers to nothing.
items.context: Opening of a letter that ranks the parts of a person; the rational part rules there as “the divine reason” rules over all things.

items.quote: One who thinks that they are unwilling to do harm, is wrong; they cannot do harm.
gives: It has no cause to do evil
items.follows: The gods are not merely unwilling to do harm; they are unable to.
items.context: On the right idea of the gods, which worship needs; “they” are the gods, whom the next section calls supreme commanders in the universe.

items.quote: even this reason which we possess is the same, because it is derived from the divine reason
gives: of one kind with it
items.follows: The reason in us is the same as the divine reason, because it comes from it.
items.context: Same opening of the letter; “this reason which we possess” is the rational part of the human soul, set beside the divine reason.

items.quote: the latter is the only thing that is not referred back to another, but rather refers all things to itself
gives: it turns everything else to its use
items.follows: The rational part answers to nothing else in a person, and everything else is referred to it.
items.context: Same opening: body serves soul and the soul's lower parts serve its primary part; “the latter” is the rational element of that part.

items.quote: the force which inheres in all the seeds of things, giving them the power to fashion each thing according to its kind
gives: the power at work
items.follows: Wisdom studies the force inside the seeds of things, which gives them the power to shape each thing.
items.context: A list of what wisdom studies, as against the crafts; “she” is wisdom going back to the beginnings of things, and “them” are the seeds.

items.quote: they all hinge on one alone, and that will be the creative cause
gives: the one source of all things
items.follows: All causes depend on one cause.
items.context: Seneca rejects Plato's and Aristotle's lists of causes; “they” are those listed causes, and the “one” is the maker, which he has just called Reason.

items.label: action
items.t: To worship what governs the world, it is enough to imitate it: to be a good man.
items.why: Marcus says to honour what is most powerful in the world. Seneca says what counts as worship enough.

support.quote: Would you win over the gods? Then be a good man. Whoever imitates them, is worshipping them sufficiently.
support.follows: To win over the gods, be a good man; imitating them is worship enough.
support.context: On how the gods should be worshipped; “them” are the gods, just called supreme commanders in the universe who control all things.

items.label: breaks
items.t: It is weakness to struggle against the order of the universe and speak ill of it, and to want to reform the gods sooner than myself.
items.why: Marcus has no passage in this section on what failing looks like. Seneca describes it, at the close of a letter on accepting what happens.

support.quote: that man is a weakling and a degenerate who struggles and maligns the order of the universe and would rather reform the gods than reform himself
support.follows: It is a weak man who fights and slanders the order of the universe and would sooner reform the gods than himself.
support.context: Close of a letter on accepting what happens as Fate's law; “that man” is whoever fights events instead of giving himself over to Fate.

items.label: why
items.t: What governs the world guards the human race, though it is sometimes unmindful of one person.
items.why: Marcus's 7.44 says that if it cares for anything in particular, it is for those who reason. Seneca says the care is for humankind and may miss one person. The two do not disagree: Marcus speaks only of a possibility.

support.quote: acting as guardians of the human race, even though they are sometimes unmindful of the individual
support.follows: The gods guard humankind but are sometimes unmindful of one person.
support.context: On what a worshipper should know of the gods; “they” are the gods, who command the universe and, he adds next, neither give nor have evil.

amend.t: , and to imitate what orders the world, by being good, is worship enough

cannot do harm / no evil / do harm
first cause / general cause / cause of

removed: God is to the world as soul is to man, a likeness of place, not “of one kind”

God and man of the same nature; same point as 92.1, already used
reason a portion of divine spirit; same point as 92.1
the universe is one and is God; same point as 95.52
care of him who governs all things; about why things last
seeming harms preserve the world, not “follow from good”; Article 3 uses it

our spirit imitates the soul of the universe; about seeking honour
reason judges good and evil in us; not about the world
honour paid to great men, not to what governs the world
