nature tempers the world by opposites; about change
all things perish in their time; about decay, not order
justice without reward; unrelated

articles.title: What I was made for

claims.t: Everything that exists, the gods included, is made for something and bears fruit of its own kind in its own time.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of everything, and both name the gods. What they say of it differs: 8.17 says it is made for something, 9.8 says it bears fruit of its kind, in its time.
claims.changed: “Made for something” and “bears fruit” are kept as two phrases, each from its own passage. Drops the horse, the vine and the sun as examples.

support.quote: Whatsoever is, was made for something: as a horse, a vine.
gives: Everything that exists
is made for something
support.follows: Everything that exists was made for something, as a horse or a vine is.

support.quote: The sun itself will say of itself, I was made for something; and so hath every god its proper function.
gives: the gods included
is made for something
support.follows: The sun would say it was made for something, and every god has a function of its own.

support.quote: Man, God, the world, every one in their kind, bear some fruits.
gives: the gods included
bears fruit of its own kind
support.follows: Man, God and the world each bear fruit of their own kind.

support.quote: All things have their proper time to bear.
gives: Everything that exists
in its own time
support.follows: Everything has its proper time to bear fruit.

claims.t: I was not made to please myself, but to keep exercising reason and fellowship. Reason by its nature turns toward other people, and its fruit is for them as well as for itself.
claims.shared: Two passages say that reason is by nature not a private thing: 6.13 calls the reasonable soul “naturally sociable”, 9.8 says reason is “of a diffusive nature” and begets itself in others. The rest is one passage each: 8.17 rules out pleasure, 6.13 names the exercise, 9.8 the fruit.
claims.changed: 8.17 only asks what I was made for and rules out pleasure. The “but” that answers it is the editor’s, and is marked.

inferences.why: 8.17 asks what I was made for and rules out only pleasure. The answer is the editor’s, taken from 6.13 and 9.8, which do not say “made for”.

support.quote: What then were then made for? to disport and delight thyself?
gives: not made to please myself
support.note: Casaubon’s text reads “were then”. The question is put to the reader.
support.follows: I should ask what I was made for, and whether it can be to amuse and please myself.

support.quote: See how even common sense and reason cannot brook it.
gives: not made to please myself
support.follows: Common sense and reason cannot accept that answer.

support.quote: is careful to preserve his own, in the continual habit and exercise both of reason and sociableness
gives: to keep exercising reason and fellowship
support.follows: Such a person takes care to keep his own soul in the constant exercise of reason and fellowship.

support.quote: he that honours a reasonable soul in general, as it is reasonable and naturally sociable
gives: Reason by its nature turns toward other people
support.follows: What is to be honoured in a soul is that it is reasonable and, by nature, sociable.

support.quote: Reason is of a diffusive nature, what itself is in itself, it begets in others, and so doth multiply.
gives: Reason by its nature turns toward other people
support.follows: Reason spreads by nature: what it is in itself it produces in others, and so it multiplies.

support.quote: As for reason, that beareth both common fruit for the use of others; and peculiar, which itself doth enjoy.
gives: its fruit is for them as well as for itself
support.follows: Reason produces something for others to use and something of its own that it enjoys.

claims.t: What looks rotten or old to me looks different to someone who knows nature well. Nature throws nothing away: she takes it back into herself and makes new things out of it, and it has something pleasing of its own.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of the rotten and the old, and both appeal to the person acquainted with nature, who sees them differently: in 8.48 he laughs at the complaint, in 3.2 he alone finds the beauty. What he sees differs: 8.48 says nature reuses such things, 3.2 says they are pleasing as they are.
claims.changed: Drops “by-products” as the common term: 8.48 has shavings and 3.2 has “accessories”, but only as comparisons. The claim now rests on the two things both passages say outright.

support.quote: whatsoever is within her that seems either corrupted, or old, or unprofitable, she can change it into herself, and of these very things can make new things
gives: What looks rotten or old
she takes it back into herself and makes new things out of it
support.follows: What seems spoiled, old or useless, nature changes into herself and makes into new things.

support.quote: one that is acquainted with the mysteries of nature, will laugh at thee for it
gives: looks different to someone who knows nature well
support.follows: Someone who knows how nature works would laugh at the question of what such things are for.

support.quote: but the nature of the universe hath no such out-place
gives: Nature throws nothing away
support.follows: Nature has nowhere outside itself to discard anything.

support.quote: So ripe olives, when they are next to putrefaction, then are they in their proper beauty.
gives: What looks rotten or old
it has something pleasing of its own
support.follows: Ripe olives are at their most beautiful when they are close to rotting.

support.quote: So will he be able to perceive the proper ripeness and beauty of old age, whether in man or woman
gives: What looks rotten or old
it has something pleasing of its own
support.follows: He will be able to see the ripeness and beauty that belong to old age, in a man or a woman.

support.quote: not credible unto every one, but unto them only who are truly and familiarly acquainted, both with nature itself, and all natural things
gives: looks different to someone who knows nature well
support.follows: Only those who know nature and natural things closely will see this; not everyone finds it believable.

support.quote: whatsoever it is that naturally doth happen to things natural, hath somewhat in itself that is pleasing and delightful
gives: it has something pleasing of its own
support.follows: Whatever happens naturally to natural things has something pleasing in it.

support.quote: even among all those things which are but mere accessories and natural appendices as it were, there will scarce appear anything unto him, wherein he will not find matter of pleasure and delight
gives: it has something pleasing of its own
support.follows: Even among nature’s side effects, he will find pleasure in almost every one.

single.label: A practice
single.t: If the cucumber is bitter, I set it aside; if brambles are in the way, I go round them. That is enough.
single.quote: Is the cucumber bitter? set it away. Brambles are in the way? avoid them. Let this suffice.
single.why: Only 8.48 gives the practice. Its second half is the next item.
single.follows: I should set the bitter thing aside, go round the obstacle, and leave it at that.

single.label: A prohibition
single.t: I do not ask of a bitter thing what it is for.
single.quote: Add not presently speaking unto thyself, What serve these things for in the world?
single.why: Only 8.48 forbids the question. Its reason is under “If I doubt it”: nature throws nothing away. Marcus does not say how this fits with 8.17, where everything was made for something.
single.follows: I should not go on to ask what such things are for.

single.label: A practice
single.t: Of each purpose and each action, taken one at a time, I see at once what its proper use is.
single.quote: in matter of purposes and actions, we must presently see what is the proper use and relation of every one
single.why: Only 7.4 asks about use action by action. It speaks of what is said and done, not of what each thing is made for, so it backs no claim.
single.follows: For every purpose and action, I should see at once what its proper use is.

decisions: Uses 6.13 and 9.8 to answer the question that 8.17 asks and leaves open. The step is marked as the editor’s: “namely” in the statement, “but” in claim 2.
Fuses 8.17 with 9.8 only on what both say: the rule covers everything, the gods included. “Made for something” is 8.17’s and “bears fruit” is 9.8’s, and the claim keeps them apart.
Fuses 6.13 with 9.8 on reason turning by its nature toward other people (“naturally sociable”, “of a diffusive nature”).
Fuses 8.48 with 3.2, the most central passage of the section, on the rotten and the old and on the person who knows nature. That nature reuses them is 8.48 alone; that they are pleasing is 3.2 alone.
Keeps 7.4 as a said-once practice. It was a witness to claim 1 without backing any of its words.
8.17 says everything was made for something; 8.48 forbids asking what a bitter thing is for. Neither passage mentions the other, and the article keeps both without reconciling them.
articles.limit: This is the smallest and loosest section: seven passages, six used. Claims 1 and 3 rest on two passages and claim 2 on three, and in each claim only part of the sentence is said by two passages: the scope in claim 1, reason’s turn toward others in claim 2, the rotten and the old and the person who knows nature in claim 3. The rest of each claim is one passage’s. That what I was made for is reason is the editor’s step; no passage of this section says it.

aside.11.5: What tragedy and comedy were instituted for. Purpose applied to drama, with nothing for a rule of life.

statement.t: Like everything that exists, the gods included, I am made for something, namely to use my reason, which by nature turns toward others.

parts.words: Like everything that exists, the gods included
to use my reason, which by nature turns toward others

inferences.why: 8.17 asks what I was made for and rules out only pleasure. That the answer is reason is the editor’s, from 6.13 and 9.8.

statement.kind: A rule, its application to me, and its hardest case
statement.form: A rule, its application to me, and the case that seems to break it. “If I doubt it” answers the objection that some things are plainly useless or flawed. “I am made for something” is said by 8.17 alone, so it carries no source line here; claim 1 shows it. That it is not for my own pleasure is also 8.17 alone and stays in claim 2.

empty.breaks: No passage in this section describes failing at one’s purpose.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, each claim gains a second author on one of its parts, and the article gains three things Marcus leaves out here: the answer to what I was made for, what failing at it looks like, and the joy that is left when pleasure is ruled out.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains its missing step. Marcus asks what I was made for and does not answer in this section; Seneca says outright that it is reason brought to perfection.

items.quote: In each thing that quality should be best for which the thing is brought into being and by which it is judged.
gives: is made for something
items.follows: In each thing, the quality that should be best is the one the thing was brought into being for.
items.context: Seneca is proving that the honourable is the only good. “That quality” is each thing’s own excellence: a vine’s yield, a stag’s speed, a dog’s scent.

items.quote: this wisdom I have declared already to be, both the good of others, and also his own
gives: its fruit is for them as well as for itself
items.follows: Wisdom is the good of other people and also the wise man’s own.
items.context: Seneca is showing that hardship cannot stop the wise man from acting. “This wisdom” is what he still practises then; “his own” means the wise man’s.

items.quote: none of the objects which vanish from our gaze and are re-absorbed into the world of things, from which they have come forth and are soon to come forth again, is annihilated
gives: she takes it back into herself
items.follows: Nothing that vanishes is destroyed: it is taken back into the world it came from and will come out of it again.
items.context: Seneca is arguing against the fear of death. The “objects” are whatever dies or disappears, which he says will return; he is not speaking of waste or flaws.

items.quote: Let us cherish and love old age; for it is full of pleasure if one knows how to use it. Fruits are most welcome when almost over
gives: it has something pleasing of its own
items.follows: Old age is full of pleasure for one who knows how to use it, as fruit is most welcome when it is almost over.
items.context: Seneca has just scolded his decaying house, his gnarled trees and an old slave, and seen his own age in them. “It” is old age; the fruit is his comparison.

items.label: why
items.t: What is peculiar to me as a human being is reason. Reason brought to perfection is the good that nature designed me for at birth, and when I fulfil it I have reached my highest good.
items.why: Marcus asks in 8.17 what I was made for and rules out pleasure, but this section never gives the answer. Seneca gives it in so many words.

support.quote: What then is peculiar to man? Reason.
gives: What is peculiar to me as a human being is reason
support.follows: What belongs to a human being alone is reason.
support.context: The same proof that the honourable is the only good. “Peculiar to man” means what a human being has and animals and plants do not.

support.quote: It is soul, and reason brought to perfection in the soul.
gives: Reason brought to perfection
support.follows: What is a person’s own is the soul, and reason brought to perfection in it.
support.context: Seneca is saying what to praise in a person: not his slaves, house or income, which are outside him. “It” is the property peculiar to a human being.

support.quote: man’s highest good is attained, if he has fulfilled the good for which nature designed him at birth
gives: the good that nature designed me for at birth
when I fulfil it I have reached my highest good
support.follows: A person reaches the highest good by fulfilling the good that nature designed him for at birth.
support.context: The close of the same argument. “The good for which nature designed him” is the reason just named, brought to perfection in the soul.

items.label: action
items.t: I am not to go without gladness. Real joy is a stern matter, and I rejoice only in what comes from my own store.
items.why: Marcus rules out pleasure as what I was made for (8.17) and says of joy only that reason enjoys its own fruit (9.8). Seneca says what joy remains and where it comes from.

support.quote: I do not wish you ever to be deprived of gladness
gives: I am not to go without gladness
support.follows: Seneca does not want his friend ever to be without gladness.
support.context: Seneca tells Lucilius to learn how to feel joy and denies he is taking pleasures from him. “Gladness” is the kind born inside a person, not a gift of chance.

support.quote: Real joy, believe me, is a stern matter.
gives: Real joy is a stern matter
support.follows: Real joy is serious, not light.
support.context: “Real joy” is that of a person who can despise death, face poverty and curb his pleasures. Seneca sets it against laughter and a cheerful face.

support.quote: rejoice only in that which comes from your own store
gives: I rejoice only in what comes from my own store
support.follows: I should rejoice only in what comes from within myself.
support.context: Said after telling Lucilius to trample what glitters outwardly. “Your own store” is, in his next words, your very self, the best part of you.

items.label: breaks
items.t: I really live when many make use of me and I make use of myself. If I creep into a hole and grow torpid, I have died before I am dead; and if I go into hiding out of fear, I am living not for myself but for my belly, my sleep and my lust.
items.why: Marcus has no passage in this section on what failing looks like. Seneca describes it twice: the man who is of use to no one, and the man who hides out of fear.

support.quote: He really lives who is made use of by many; he really lives who makes use of himself.
gives: I really live when many make use of me and I make use of myself
support.follows: To be really alive is to be of use to many and to make use of oneself.
support.context: The letter attacks living for the belly. “He” is set against those who obey their appetites, some of whom Seneca has just counted among the dead.

support.quote: Those men, however, who creep into a hole and grow torpid are no better off in their homes than if they were in their tombs.
gives: If I creep into a hole and grow torpid
support.follows: People who hide away and go numb are no better off at home than in a tomb.
support.context: “Those men” are the opposite of the man of use to many: people who withdraw into sloth, in a letter about living for the belly.

support.quote: he has died before he is dead
gives: I have died before I am dead
support.follows: Such a man has died before his death.
support.context: “He” is the same torpid man. Seneca says his name may be carved on the lintel of his house as on a tomb.

support.quote: who through fear has taken to concealment
gives: if I go into hiding out of fear
support.follows: The man in question has gone into hiding out of fear.
support.context: Seneca is at the villa of Vatia, who was famous only for his leisure, and separates leisure from hiding. “Who” is the man fled from affairs and from men.

support.quote: this person is not living for himself; he is living for his belly, his sleep, and his lust
gives: I am living not for myself but for my belly, my sleep and my lust
support.follows: A man who hides like that does not live for himself; he lives for his belly, his sleep and his lust.
support.context: “This person” is the man who has hidden from affairs and people out of fear and failed desires. It is not anyone at rest, nor anyone enjoying himself.

amend.t: , for reason brought to perfection is the good that nature designed me for at birth

for pleasure; pleasure with cattle or animals
common good / good of others / live for
acquainted with nature / secrets of nature

rejected.why: was in use twice; its “appointed times” are those of birth and destruction, not of bearing fruit, and 36.10 says the reuse more fully

articles.title: What the whole sends in its season

claims.role: What comes is good, and on time
claims.t: What the whole brings me is good for me, and it comes at the right time: nothing that is timely for the whole is too early or too late for me.
claims.shared: Both passages say that what nature brings is good for the one it is brought to (10.21: “good for each”; 4.19: “fruit to me”). Both add the time: 10.21 that it is good when nature brings it, 4.19 that what is timely for the universe is never too early or too late for me.
claims.changed: 10.21 says “each”; the claim says “me”, as 4.19 does. 4.19 speaks to the universe and to nature as “you”; the claim speaks about them and calls both “the whole”, 10.21’s word.

support.quote: What the nature of the whole brings to each is good for each
gives: What the whole brings me is good for me
support.follows: Whatever the nature of the whole brings to anyone is good for that one.

support.quote: it is good at the time when nature brings it
gives: it comes at the right time
support.follows: It is good at the time nature brings it.

support.quote: Nature, everything your seasons bear is fruit to me.
gives: What the whole brings me is good for me
support.follows: I count whatever nature’s seasons bear as fruit.

support.quote: Nothing that is timely for you is too early or too late for me.
gives: it comes at the right time
nothing that is timely for the whole is too early or too late for me
support.follows: What comes at the universe’s right time does not come at a wrong time for me.

claims.t: I take the universe’s side: what it loves to bring about, I love along with it, and whatever fits well with it fits well with me.
claims.shared: Both passages are spoken to the universe, and in both the speaker puts himself on its side: in 10.22 he loves along with it; in 4.19 what fits it fits him.
claims.changed: Both passages say “you” to the universe; the claim speaks about it. “I take the universe’s side” is the editor’s summary of what the two say in their own words.

support.quote: the universe loves to bring about whatever is to come
gives: what it loves to bring about
support.follows: The universe loves to bring about whatever is going to happen.

support.quote: So I say to the universe: “I love along with you.”
gives: I take the universe’s side
I love along with it
support.follows: Marcus tells the universe that he loves along with it.

support.quote: Universe, everything that fits well with you fits well with me.
gives: I take the universe’s side
whatever fits well with it fits well with me
support.follows: Whatever fits the universe well fits Marcus well.

single.label: Different parts, one work
single.t: The sun does not do the rain’s part, and no god does another’s. The parts of the world differ, and they work together toward the same thing.
single.quote: Surely the sun does not think it should do the rain’s part? Or Asclepius the part of the fruit-bearing goddess? And what of each of the stars? Are they not different, yet working together toward the same thing?
single.why: Only this passage speaks of the parts of the world and their separate tasks. No second passage of the section says it, so it is not fused.
single.follows: Each power keeps to its own part; the parts differ and work together toward the same thing.

single.label: One source
single.t: Everything is from nature, in nature, and goes into nature.
single.quote: All things from you, all things in you, all things into you.
single.why: Only this passage says it. It names a source, a place and a destination; it does not say that things work toward an end.
single.follows: All things are from nature, in nature and go into nature.

single.label: A practice
single.t: As one man says “Dear city of Cecrops” of Athens, I say “Dear city of Zeus”.
single.quote: One man says, “Dear city of Cecrops.” But you, will you not say, “Dear city of Zeus”?
single.why: Only this passage gives words to say. They are kept as the article’s practice.
single.follows: If one man can call Athens dear, I am asked to say “Dear city of Zeus”.

single.label: A practice · how to pray
single.t: If I pray, I pray simply and like a free person, as the Athenians prayed for rain on their land.
single.quote: A prayer of the Athenians: “Rain, rain, dear Zeus, down on the ploughland of the Athenians and the plains.” Either one should not pray, or one should pray like this: simply and like a free person.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of prayer. It says how to pray, not for whom.
single.follows: If one prays at all, one should pray as in this prayer: simply and like a free person.

single.label: Meeting an obstacle
single.t: When something stands in my way, I do not force my way and I do not fall. I stand and give light to whatever receives it; what gives the light no passage deprives itself of it.
single.quote: It should not lean on the obstacles it meets with force or like a torrent, nor fall down, but stand and light up whatever receives it. For whatever does not give the beam passage will deprive itself of the beam.
single.why: Only this passage says how to meet what resists me. It shows what failing looks like, forcing or falling, and the way back.
single.follows: Meeting an obstacle, thought should neither force its way nor fall, but stand and light up what receives it.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 10.21 is 10.20, 10.22 is 10.21, 4.19 is 4.23, 6.38 is 6.43 and 8.54 is 8.57; 5.7 is the same.
Reads “the nature of the whole” (10.21), the universe and nature addressed in 4.19, and the universe of 10.22 as one whole.

Keeps only two fused claims. In claim 1 both passages say that what nature brings is good for the one it is brought to, and both speak of its time. In claim 2 the words the two share, “I take the universe’s side”, are the editor’s summary of two sentences spoken to the universe. The parts of the world working together (6.38) and all things from, in and into nature (4.19) are each said by one passage and stand alone.
Withdraws the earlier claim that I pray “for everyone, not for myself alone”. It rested on a clause Casaubon added to 5.7; the Greek ends at “simply and like a free person”.
Reads “Dear city of Zeus” (4.19) as said of the world. The Greek does not say what the city of Zeus is.
Leaves out the poet’s line and the last sentence of 10.22, a remark on a Greek turn of phrase.
articles.limit: Article 3 already says that I accept whatever happens. What this article adds is the time: what comes is good when it comes, never too early or too late. It adds little else. Six passages give two fused claims, and 4.19 feeds both, so the article leans on one passage. It states a trust and does not argue for it.

statement.t: What the whole brings me is good for me and comes at the right time, so I take its side.

parts.words: What the whole brings me is good for me

inferences.why: No passage joins these two. In 10.22 Marcus’s own “So” runs from the universe’s love to his; the step from “good for me” to taking its side is the editor’s.

statement.kind: A ground and the stance that answers it
statement.form: Claim 1 is the ground: what the whole brings is good for me and comes at the right time. Claim 2 is the stance Marcus takes toward the universe. The “so” that joins them in the statement is the editor’s.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section considers that what the whole brings might not be good for me. The article states the trust and does not argue for it.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, taking the universe’s side gains two witnesses, and the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: the hard things, paid willingly as a tax; words for a setback; a test for prayer; how to stand under pain; an answer when a death seems too early; and what holds if I doubt it. He backs nothing in the first claim, and he limits the second: he does not crave hardship itself.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and takes in the hard things: I take the whole’s side, and what is hard in what it brings I pay willingly, as a tax on being alive. He does not say that I should want it.

items.quote: I have trained myself not merely to obey God, but to agree with His decisions
gives: I take the universe’s side
items.follows: Seneca has trained himself to agree with what God decides, and not only to obey it.
items.context: Seneca answers a complaining Lucilius. “His decisions” are God’s: the illness and losses Seneca has just listed as his own, which he says come by order and not by accident.

items.quote: Let man be pleased with whatever has pleased God
gives: I take the universe’s side
items.follows: A person should be pleased with whatever has pleased God.
items.context: On the inner defence against Fortune: not chafing at what happens to one. “Whatever has pleased God” is whatever happens, including what seems to bring harm.

items.label: action
items.t: The hard things are a tax on being alive, and I pay it willingly. Whatever makes me groan or shrink back is part of that tax, and I do not hope or try to escape it.
items.why: In this section Marcus calls what comes fruit and says it is timely; none of his passages names the hard part of it. Seneca names it, and calls it a tax, not a fruit. He says how to receive it: willingly. He does not say that I should want it.

support.quote: I shall pay up all my taxes willingly.
gives: I pay it willingly
support.follows: Seneca will pay every tax he owes, and pay it willingly.
support.context: From Letter 96, where Seneca tells Lucilius to agree with what God decides. The “taxes” are not money: the next sentence says they are everything in life that makes us groan or recoil.

support.quote: Now all the things which cause us to groan or recoil, are part of the tax of life—things, my dear Lucilius, which you should never hope and never seek to escape.
gives: The hard things are a tax on being alive
Whatever makes me groan or shrink back is part of that tax
I do not hope or try to escape it
support.follows: What makes us groan or recoil is part of the price of living, and we should neither hope nor try to escape it.
support.context: Said to Lucilius, who had feared for his life in an illness. The things that make us groan are the illness, losses, toil and fear listed just before.

items.label: practice
items.t: Whenever something turns out against what I expected, I say to myself: “Heaven decreed better.”
items.why: Marcus gives words to say of the world: “Dear city of Zeus”. Seneca gives words to say at each setback. They say that what was decided is better than what I expected; they do not say, as 10.21 does, that it is good for me.

support.quote: say to yourself, whenever things turn out contrary to your expectation: “Heaven decreed better!”
gives: Whenever something turns out against what I expected
Heaven decreed better
support.follows: When things go against what I expected, I should tell myself that the gods decided better.
support.context: On holding what Fortune gives without leaning on it. He first offers “Heaven decreed it otherwise” for every mishap, then this, as braver and nearer the truth.

items.label: practice
items.t: I speak with God as if other people were listening. The day I ask for nothing that I could not ask for openly, I am free of my desires.
items.why: 5.7 says to pray simply and like a free person, and gives no test. Seneca gives one, and ties it to freedom as well: whoever asks only for what he could ask for openly is free of his desires.

support.quote: Know that thou art freed from all desires when thou hast reached such a point that thou prayest to God for nothing except what thou canst pray for openly.
gives: The day I ask for nothing that I could not ask for openly, I am free of my desires
support.follows: A person is free of his desires once he prays only for what he could pray for openly.
support.context: Seneca has just told Lucilius to drop his old prayers and ask for a sound mind. The saying is Athenodorus’s; to pray “openly” is to ask only for what others may hear.

support.quote: Live among men as if God beheld you; speak with God as if men were listening
gives: I speak with God as if other people were listening
support.follows: I should live as if God saw me and speak with God as if people heard me.
support.context: Seneca’s own advice, drawn from that saying: people whisper to the gods the base wishes they hide from men. To “speak with God” is to pray.

items.label: breaks
items.t: In pain or illness, if I give way to my suffering, it beats me. It is like a wall falling toward me: if I hold my ground and push against it, it is forced back.
items.why: 8.54 is about an obstacle in my way: I do not force it and I do not fall. Seneca speaks of something else, pain and illness that press on me, and says to stand up to them. He resists suffering that has to be borne; he does not attack an obstacle, so the two do not conflict.

support.quote: if he once gives way, he will be vanquished; but if he strives against his sufferings, he will conquer.
gives: if I give way to my suffering, it beats me
support.follows: Whoever gives way to his sufferings is beaten; whoever strives against them wins.
support.context: A letter on bearing illness and pain, to Lucilius, who is ill; Seneca recalls his own sickness. “He” is anyone in the midst of troubles, striving against his sufferings.

support.quote: but if you hold your ground and make up your mind to push against it, it will be forced back.
gives: if I hold my ground and push against it, it is forced back
support.follows: What leans on me is forced back if I hold my ground and push against it.
support.context: Same passage. “It” is a falling ruin that leans on you: Seneca’s image for pain, which presses harder on the one who backs away from it.

items.label: breaks
items.role: When a death seems too early
items.t: When a death seems to come too early, I ask which is fairer: that I obey nature, or that nature obey me. How soon I leave a place I must leave anyway makes no difference, and a short life can be a perfect one.
items.why: The time is this article’s own point: nothing is too early or too late for me. Seneca meets it in one case only, a death that seems to come too soon, and his answer is not Marcus’s. He does not say the time was right; he says the length of a life does not decide whether it is complete.

support.quote: do you consider it fairer that you should obey Nature, or that Nature should obey you? And what difference does it make how soon you depart from a place which you must depart from sooner or later?
gives: which is fairer: that I obey nature, or that nature obey me
How soon I leave a place I must leave anyway makes no difference
support.follows: Seneca asks which is fairer, that I obey nature or that nature obey me, and what difference it makes how soon I leave a place I must leave.
support.context: Lucilius mourned the philosopher Metronax as dead too soon; Seneca calls such complaints railing at Fate. The “place which you must depart from” is life.

support.quote: Just as one of small stature can be a perfect man, so a life of small compass can be a perfect life.
gives: a short life can be a perfect one
support.follows: A short life can be a perfect life, as a small man can be a perfect man.
support.context: Same letter: a life is to be measured by what was done in it, not by how long it lasted. “A life of small compass” is a short life.

items.label: doubt
items.role: Even if it is a disaster
items.t: Even if what comes is a disaster, a loss or a wrong, it has no more power over my virtue than a cloud has over the sun: my virtue shines less brightly, but it is no smaller.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section asks what holds if what comes is not good for me. Seneca’s answer is that even a disaster cannot make virtue smaller. He uses the sun for it, as 8.54 uses a sunbeam for the mind.

support.quote: obstacles take nothing away from virtue; it is no smaller, but merely shines with less brilliancy.
gives: my virtue shines less brightly, but it is no smaller
support.follows: Obstacles take nothing away from virtue; it only shines less brightly.
support.context: Seneca argues that a good man is happy even under misfortune. “Obstacles” are what stands in virtue’s way as an object stands before the sun, which is no smaller for it.

support.quote: Disasters, therefore, and losses, and wrongs, have only the same power over virtue that a cloud has over the sun.
gives: Even if what comes is a disaster, a loss or a wrong
it has no more power over my virtue than a cloud has over the sun
support.follows: Disasters, losses and wrongs have no more power over virtue than a cloud has over the sun.
support.context: The conclusion of that comparison: a cloud hides the sun and takes nothing from it. “Virtue” is the good man’s, which Seneca holds to be his whole good.

items.t: Seneca stops short of Marcus’s word “love”. He agrees with what God decides and receives it without complaint (Ep. 96.2), but he says he is not so mad as to crave a hardship: what he wants is the virtue that bears it. This limits the claim and does not contradict it. He would rather be spared beforehand and agrees once it comes; and of his own death he says he should desire whatever circumstances demand (Ep. 61.3).

support.quote: Nor am I so mad as to crave illness; but if I must suffer illness, I shall desire that I may do nothing which shows lack of restraint, and nothing that is unmanly.
support.follows: Seneca does not want illness; if he must be ill, what he wants is to do nothing unrestrained or weak in it.
support.context: Lucilius asked whether every good is desirable, since bravery under torture is a good. Seneca separates the hardship, which he does not want, from his conduct in it.

support.quote: The conclusion is, not that hardships are desirable, but that virtue is desirable, which enables us patiently to endure hardships.
support.follows: What is desirable is not hardship but the virtue that lets us bear hardship patiently.
support.context: Seneca’s own summing-up of his answer to that question. The “hardships” are the torture, war and illness he has just named.

support.quote: Let us therefore so set our minds in order that we may desire whatever is demanded of us by circumstances
support.follows: I should bring my mind to want whatever circumstances require of me.
support.context: Seneca, now old, writes that dying well means dying gladly and that one should do nothing unwillingly. What circumstances demand is, above all, his death.

amend.t: ; what is hard in it I pay willingly, as a tax on being alive
; but I do not crave hardship itself, and what I want, if it must come, is the virtue to bear it

searches: timely, too early, too late, untimely, appointed time

rejected.why: About everything perishing: the “appointed times” are those of birth, growth and destruction, and the “same goal” is dissolution. Says nothing of a time that is right for me. Both old pieces removed.

Sets a puzzle (how can goods be equal if they are of three kinds?) that the letter answers by calling them equal. Its rule on prayer was aimed at a claim now withdrawn. Ep. 67.4 asks the question directly.
Nature rules by changing seasons, storm after calm. Says the soul must adjust to this law, not that what comes is good for me or on time.
Do not rail at Nature; endure what cannot be reformed. Already in Article 3, and about enduring, not about taking the universe’s side.
“Welcome our orders with energy”, following a universe into which future sufferings are woven. Says what 96.2 and 74.20 say; a third witness for the same words was not needed.
Cleanthes’s prayer. “The willing soul Fate leads” argues that refusing is useless; Article 3 uses it for that. Here it would only repeat obedience.
The great soul has given himself over to Fate. Same point as 96.2, in a letter already used in Article 3.
Its first half (apparent harms work for the preservation of the world) is about the good of the world, not good for me; used in Article 3. Only “pleased with whatever has pleased God” is used here.
Fortune gives only the raw material of goods and ills. A possible limit on “good for me”, but it is about Fortune, and three sections on he says Heaven decreed better. Not a clear disagreement.
“Beholden to the seasons”, though they were not apportioned for my benefit. About gratitude for goods shared with all, in a letter on rulers and peace.
The good man endures whatever happens because it comes by divine law. An argument that only the honourable is good; about enduring.
The wise man wills what necessity is about to force on him. About leaving life; 61.3 says the same more generally and is quoted.
Endure “willingly and with alacrity”: the oath of one who has enlisted as a good man. About enduring trials, not about what they are.
If God is pleased to add another day, welcome it. Welcomes a gain, in a letter on living each day as the last.
The wise man taught us to welcome the gifts of chance as divine commands. One item in a list about what philosophy discovered; no context of its own.
The perfect man as citizen and soldier of the universe, taking what happens as his orders. A portrait of acceptance as duty; nearer to Article 3.
A prayer that Fortune not keep Lucilius in luxury. Against softness, said for a friend; not a wish for hardship.
Even an untimely death leaves a full life. Same point as Ep. 93, which is quoted and is fuller.
On the untimely dead: every life is short beside eternity. A different consolation; does not speak of the right time.
Wheat has its good only when ripe. About when a thing’s own good exists, not about what comes to me.
Olive trees “bearing fruit in due season”. Literal farming.
We are parts and members of God. Whole and part, but it backs neither claim, and the said-once items on the parts of the world take no backing.
We are the parts of one great body. About what people owe one another; Article 1’s subject.
Pray for a sound mind and good health of soul. Says what to pray for; 5.7 is about how. The next section, 10.5, is used.
Foolish to pray for a sound mind when you can get it from yourself. About where understanding comes from.
Stop thinking prayers can bend divine decrees. A line of Virgil used against the fear of death; 5.7 does not say prayer is useless.
In praying for a life of honour I pray also for the hardships it may include. Shows he can pray for hardship indirectly; left out to keep the item to his direct answer in 67.4.
Do not regard obstacles to an honourable act as evils. “Obstacle” here is a hindrance to a deed, in an argument that honourable acts are voluntary.
Obey God cheerfully, Fortune defiantly. Already in Article 3.
